text: A linear chain of three masses: a learning bar at one end, a community commons at the other, and a civic hinge between them. The hinge gathers the school's public face (arrival, the office, the arts and the library) and acts as front door and crossroads, so every passage between learning and commons crosses it. Aims to give the school one legible front where visitors, families and daily student movement meet, while keeping classrooms quiet at the far end of the chain and the commons reachable for community use.

A compact closed cluster in which the shared realm is layered vertically: the commons volume forms the base and an arts loft rides on its roof, making one cultural block for gathering, performance and making. A civic block crowned by the library and a plain academic bar complete a triangle, each mass joined to both others. Seeks to make arts and performance a visible community destination stacked with the commons, and to give every mass a direct indoor link so daily movement stays short and sheltered.

Three free-standing pavilions on shared grounds with no built connections, read as a small campus. A self-sufficient learning pavilion also holds daily care. A community pavilion for athletics and dining can open on its own. A low civic-arts pavilion sits at arrival with the library above the office. Movement between the pavilions is outdoors. Aims to let the community pavilion operate after hours without opening the rest of the school, and to keep students' daily needs, including the nurse, inside the learning pavilion.

The commons is the central heart, with a civic front on one side and a learning wing on the other, each joined only through the heart. Arrival leads into the shared volume, and the learning wing lies beyond it, buffered from public entry. The arts move into the learning wing as part of daily teaching. Seeks to make the commons the school's social centre and community entry point, while keeping the learning wing and its arts studios away from visitor traffic.

A tall academy holds classrooms over the front office with the library at its crown. Beside it, a care-and-making house pairs specialized learning with the nurse and the arts. Together with the commons, the three masses close a loop around a shared court, each joined directly to the other two. Aims to put leadership and the library inside the main learning building, and to give students with special needs a dedicated house with nearby medical care and hands-on arts rooms.

A low civic gateway stands between a three-storey learning bar and a community hall and forms the only enclosed passage between them. Everyone arrives through the gateway, where the school's front and its making and reading spaces meet visitors; classrooms extend behind it on one side and the shared hall on the other. Aims to give staff a single supervised threshold controlling access to both classrooms and hall, and to let evening visitors reach the hall and arts without entering classroom corridors.

A low civic gateway stands between a three-storey learning bar and a community hall and forms the only enclosed passage between them. Everyone arrives through the gateway, where the school's front and its making and reading spaces meet visitors; classrooms extend behind it on one side and the shared hall on the other.

A shared heart gathers the school's communal life: the hall for play, dining and assembly, crowned by a studio loft for art and music. Two wings, one of classrooms and one forming the school's front with its inclusive support, attach only to the heart, so all movement between them passes through it. Seeks to make daily crossings through the heart a social routine that brings students from both wings together at lunch, assembly and arts, and to give the community one focal destination.

Two wings, one of classrooms and one forming the school's front with its inclusive support, attach only to the heart, so all movement between them passes through it.

One self-contained school bar carries the whole teaching day, rising from the front office and specialist support at its foot through classrooms to a reading crown. Two freestanding pavilions, a community hall and a making-and-maintenance workshop, stand apart on shared grounds and are reached outdoors. Aims to let the hall and workshop open to the community and be phased independently, while keeping the instructional day secure inside a single enclosed bar.

Three ranges close around a courtyard and join at every corner into a continuous indoor loop: a tall learning range, a low civic and arts front, and a commons range whose hall is crowned by a reading loft that looks down into the court. Seeks a protected outdoor room that every part of the school opens onto, with indoor circulation around it, and places reading at the social centre above shared dining.

Three ranges close around a courtyard and join at every corner into a continuous indoor loop: a tall learning range, a low civic and arts front, and a commons range whose hall is crowned by a reading loft that looks down into the court.

Classrooms stay low and close to the ground in a two-storey learning bar, flanked by the hall on one side and, on the other, a compact three-storey civic tower that stacks the school's front, its specialist support and a library crown as the building's vertical marker. Aims to keep every classroom within one stair of the ground and close to the hall, while giving the school a clear civic address and grouping supervision, nursing and special education support.

Classrooms stay low and close to the ground in a two-storey learning bar, flanked by the hall on one side and, on the other, a compact three-storey civic tower that stacks the school's front, its specialist support and a library crown as the building's vertical marker.

A linear sequence of three parts: a quiet learning bar at one end, an assembly hall at the other, and a compact civic hinge between them. The hinge is the front door and the school's cultural core, stacking arts and the library over the front office, so every passage between classrooms and the hall crosses the public centre of the school. Aims to give visitors one supervised arrival point at the middle of the school, buffer classrooms from hall noise, and let arts and library programs anchor community use next to the hall.

A centralized plan: the hall is the heart, and two wings plug into it from opposite sides. One wing is a complete learning house with its own arts rooms; the other is a small front-of-house wing carrying the office with the library above. The wings meet only through the heart, never directly. Seeks to make lunch, assemblies and PE the daily crossroads of the school community while letting the learning house run as a self-contained teaching building with arts beside classrooms.

A compact cluster: three three-storey masses linked to one another around a shared courtyard. The hall is not a low shed but a full-height block, crowned by an arts loft above its service side looking onto the stage. A learning bar and a civic house complete the ring, the civic house keeping specialized learning close to the office and nurse. Aims to bring every mass to three floors, allow indoor movement between any two parts, and join arts with the hall into one performance and community venue.

The hall is not a low shed but a full-height block, crowned by an arts loft above its service side looking onto the stage. A learning bar and a civic house complete the ring, the civic house keeping specialized learning close to the office and nurse.

Two parallel learning bars joined to each other form the school proper, the library crowning the classroom bar. The hall stands apart as a freestanding community building on shared grounds. One bar is the classroom house; the other is a front and inclusion house that pairs the office with specialized learning. Seeks to let the hall open independently for community use, concentrate school security in the joined bars, and put the library at the top of the classroom house where most students learn.

Two parallel learning bars joined to each other form the school proper, the library crowning the classroom bar. The hall stands apart as a freestanding community building on shared grounds. One bar is the classroom house; the other is a front and inclusion house that pairs the office with specialized learning.

One large learning block holds almost the whole school day, with the front door at its base and the library at its crown. A low, single-storey workshop pavilion for making and building service is the hinge to the hall, so hands-on work and service sit between learning and assembly. Aims to keep most students and staff in one building with short vertical trips, while giving messy, noisy arts work and building service their own ground-level place beside the hall and kitchen.

One large learning block holds almost the whole school day, with the front door at its base and the library at its crown. A low, single-storey workshop pavilion for making and building service is the hinge to the hall, so hands-on work and service sit between learning and assembly.

The school is conceived as two distinct daily environments joined by a shared assembly crossing. One is a vertical academic house for ordinary teaching; the other is a smaller care and cultural house for focused support, making, and reading. The commons between them is a destination in its own right, with a defined passage across its perimeter linking the two houses. The scheme seeks to make communal activity a deliberate transition between different learning environments while allowing specialized support to retain an identifiable and quieter home.

The care house may require substantial footprint to combine specialized teaching, administration and ground-level arts.
Movement between the two end houses depends entirely on the commons connection.
The governing GFA and footprint proportions have not been demonstrated.

A raised cultural house acts as an inhabited bridge between a teaching house and a communal base. Unlike a compact triangular cluster, the school is organized as two separated destinations connected by a third elevated cultural layer. The bridge provides a distinct shared destination while the hall remains an independent double-height volume below its own roof, not the supporting base for an arts loft. Seeks to make creative and reading activities a visible connection between learning and assembly, encouraging shared cultural use while distinguishing public gatherings from the quieter daily teaching environment.

The separate double-height commons must satisfy the overall gross-floor-area target and individual footprint proportions.
The bridge concept requires a viable structural and circulation interpretation without assuming unsupported site geometry.

A dedicated cultural threshold stands between two sharply different destinations: a consolidated academic house and a communal assembly hall. Unlike a conventional civic gateway, the threshold is primarily a place of making, student care and reading, while the school's administrative front remains embedded within the academic house. This separates the symbolic cultural entrance from the operational point of school oversight. The scheme seeks to give creative learning a recognizable shared address while allowing administration to remain closely tied to classrooms and placing community assembly beyond a cultural transition.

Two distinct teaching houses stand alongside a third, shared civic spine. Rather than treating specialized learning as an appendage of general classrooms, the houses are peers, each directly connected to the spine but not to one another. The spine combines the school's public threshold and collective gathering spaces, making a common institutional address for two different learning environments. The scheme seeks to establish equivalent identities for general and specialized learning while concentrating shared services and community activities at a common, supervised point of access.

The school is conceived as a paired everyday teaching and assembly building alongside a separate, vertically organized inclusion house. The attached pair establishes the collective school routine, while the independent house offers another scale of occupation for focused support and small-group learning. Their relationship is that of neighboring institutions on shared grounds, not an enclosed three-part circulation network. The scheme seeks to provide a distinct setting for intensive support while retaining direct academic access to communal activities and allowing the separate house to establish its own daily rhythm.

Three independent school houses face a common outdoor forum, making the open ground the organizing centre rather than an enclosed corridor. A taller teaching house establishes one edge, a separate support and cultural house forms another, and the communal hall completes the constellation. Each building keeps its own threshold, so relationships occur through the shared exterior rather than constructed links. The scheme seeks to encourage outdoor encounters among different school communities while maintaining independent identities and operational boundaries for teaching, support and collective events.

Two parallel inhabited ranges establish separate but complementary school streets. One is a continuous teaching environment; the other combines arrival, cultural activity and community gathering into a layered public range. A smaller support house connects the two at one end, creating a sheltered circulation circuit without enclosing a courtyard. The assembly volume anchors the public range rather than occupying an independent central block. Seeks to distinguish everyday teaching circulation from community activity while retaining an enclosed route between them, with a support house providing a controlled transition for students and visitors.

Two teaching-related houses form a paired educational precinct, while the commons stands apart as a separate community destination. The principal classroom house establishes the daily academic center. A neighboring inclusion and civic house accommodates more individualized learning and public-facing support. The freestanding hall belongs to the same school grounds but is not part of an enclosed circulation loop or courtyard perimeter. Seeks to establish distinguishable learning environments for general and individualized teaching, while allowing the community commons to operate as a separate destination without occupying the center of school circulation.

A communal crossing separates two complementary educational territories: a general learning house and a specialized learning house. The gym and dining volume occupies the crossing, becoming the only enclosed route between the two. Both educational houses rise above a lower communal middle, giving the school a paired identity rather than one dominant academic center. The specialized house also establishes the school's civic face. The scheme seeks to make shared activity an intentional meeting point between general and specialized education while allowing each teaching territory to retain a distinct internal organization and atmosphere.

A layered school is organized around a controlled civic filter separating a concentrated teaching house from a tall shared-activity house. The middle building is conceived as a sequence of thresholds rather than simply a connector: it mediates between protected daily learning and collective events. Above the gathering volumes, specialist teaching forms a distinct upper setting within the communal house. The scheme seeks to maintain a clear administrative threshold between teaching and community activity while placing specialist support within reach of communal learning and shared facilities.

The school revolves around an inclusive commons conceived as a shared threshold rather than a conventional assembly hall. Everyday teaching approaches it from one side, and the school's civic and cultural activities approach from the other. Specialist support is embedded in this collective middle ground, allowing the commons to act as a carefully managed meeting place between academic and community routines. The scheme seeks to make supported participation in collective school life central to the educational experience while retaining distinct academic and civic domains on either side of the shared threshold.

A three-storey cultural threshold separates two different institutional worlds: a concentrated academy and a communal house that combines gathering with specialized care. The threshold is the only built passage between them, conceived as a sequence of creative and reading environments rather than a conventional administrative crossroads. Its layered activities give the intermediate building an inhabited identity of its own. The scheme seeks to buffer general classrooms from large communal events while making cultural activities a shared destination and keeping specialized support close to collective school life.

The school separates into a quieter learning island and a connected public dock. The learning island contains the everyday educational community, including specialized instruction, but remains physically independent. The public dock is a paired composition: a large gathering hall directly attached to a taller cultural and administrative house. Shared grounds connect these two realms without an enclosed route between school teaching and civic activities. The scheme seeks to establish a strong communal destination for cultural events and school gathering while protecting the teaching environment from the circulation and activity associated with larger public functions.

Three equally developed building parts form an interconnected school with several ways to move between daily teaching, shared cultural life and assembly. Rather than organizing circulation around one obligatory crossroads or courtyard, the scheme uses direct links between every pair to create alternative internal routes. Each part maintains its own identity while participating in a continuous network of school life. The scheme seeks to distribute movement across multiple connections, give staff alternative routes between activities and reduce dependence on a single communal passage during daily transitions.

A teaching house, a specialist cultural house and a collective activity house form a three-part academic neighborhood. None is subordinated to a dominant school bar or a small workshop hinge. All three connect directly, allowing daily school life to circulate among complementary destinations while keeping large assembly activities outside the main teaching house. The scheme seeks to create a balanced set of learning destinations, giving specialized teaching an identifiable place without separating it from general classrooms, administrative care or collective school activities.

The scheme seeks to make academic life the organizing center of school movement while giving cultural activities and large gatherings distinct destinations with different levels of activity.

The school is divided into two architectural territories: a self-contained inclusive academy and a paired civic precinct. The academy is deliberately complete as a daily learning environment, while a separate commons and cultural house form one connected ensemble for gathering, making and reading. Outdoor movement between the territories becomes a legible change from academic routine to collective school life. The scheme seeks to concentrate daily teaching and care within one building while allowing cultural and community functions to operate as a distinct, directly connected precinct.

Three vertically developed houses form a mutually connected cluster organized by an exchange of everyday activities rather than by a single central hall. The learning house acts as the stable academic anchor; a civic house provides a distinct arrival and cultural address; and a communal house accommodates collective events. Direct connections between every pair allow several internal paths through the cluster. The strategy seeks to offer alternative circulation paths between classrooms, shared activities and school services while maintaining a coherent academic home for both general and specialized teaching.

A learning cloister is formed by a pair of directly joined low ranges, one devoted to sustained teaching and the other to the school's cultural and administrative life. The joined ranges establish an inward-facing academic precinct without requiring a complete enclosed courtyard. A separate communal hall remains an independent pavilion, approached across shared outdoor ground rather than through an internal school corridor. The scheme seeks to establish a cohesive low-rise teaching precinct, preserve a sense of collective outdoor space, and give community activities an independent identity.

A linear chain of three masses: a learning bar at one end, a community commons at the other, and a civic hinge between them. The hinge gathers the school's public face (arrival, the office, the arts and the library) and acts as front door and crossroads, so every passage between learning and commons crosses it.

A compact closed cluster in which the shared realm is layered vertically: the commons volume forms the base and an arts loft rides on its roof, making one cultural block for gathering, performance and making. A civic block crowned by the library and a plain academic bar complete a triangle, each mass joined to both others.

Three free-standing pavilions on shared grounds with no built connections, read as a small campus. A self-sufficient learning pavilion also holds daily care. A community pavilion for athletics and dining can open on its own. A low civic-arts pavilion sits at arrival with the library above the office. Movement between the pavilions is outdoors.

The commons is the central heart, with a civic front on one side and a learning wing on the other, each joined only through the heart. Arrival leads into the shared volume, and the learning wing lies beyond it, buffered from public entry. The arts move into the learning wing as part of daily teaching.

A tall academy holds classrooms over the front office with the library at its crown. Beside it, a care-and-making house pairs specialized learning with the nurse and the arts. Together with the commons, the three masses close a loop around a shared court, each joined directly to the other two.

A low civic gateway stands between a three-storey learning bar and a community hall and forms the only enclosed passage between them. Everyone arrives through the gateway, where the school's front and its making and reading spaces meet visitors; classrooms extend behind it on one side and the shared hall on the other.

A shared heart gathers the school's communal life: the hall for play, dining and assembly, crowned by a studio loft for art and music. Two wings, one of classrooms and one forming the school's front with its inclusive support, attach only to the heart, so all movement between them passes through it.

One self-contained school bar carries the whole teaching day, rising from the front office and specialist support at its foot through classrooms to a reading crown. Two freestanding pavilions, a community hall and a making-and-maintenance workshop, stand apart on shared grounds and are reached outdoors.

Three ranges close around a courtyard and join at every corner into a continuous indoor loop: a tall learning range, a low civic and arts front, and a commons range whose hall is crowned by a reading loft that looks down into the court.

Classrooms stay low and close to the ground in a two-storey learning bar, flanked by the hall on one side and, on the other, a compact three-storey civic tower that stacks the school's front, its specialist support and a library crown as the building's vertical marker.

A linear sequence of three parts: a quiet learning bar at one end, an assembly hall at the other, and a compact civic hinge between them. The hinge is the front door and the school's cultural core, stacking arts and the library over the front office, so every passage between classrooms and the hall crosses the public centre of the school.

A centralized plan: the hall is the heart, and two wings plug into it from opposite sides. One wing is a complete learning house with its own arts rooms; the other is a small front-of-house wing carrying the office with the library above. The wings meet only through the heart, never directly.

A compact cluster: three three-storey masses linked to one another around a shared courtyard. The hall is not a low shed but a full-height block, crowned by an arts loft above its service side looking onto the stage. A learning bar and a civic house complete the ring, the civic house keeping specialized learning close to the office and nurse.

Two parallel learning bars joined to each other form the school proper, the library crowning the classroom bar. The hall stands apart as a freestanding community building on shared grounds. One bar is the classroom house; the other is a front and inclusion house that pairs the office with specialized learning.

One large learning block holds almost the whole school day, with the front door at its base and the library at its crown. A low, single-storey workshop pavilion for making and building service is the hinge to the hall, so hands-on work and service sit between learning and assembly.

Teaching spaces occupy a modest two-level structure that maintains a strong connection to the site. An assembly facility borders one side, while the opposite side meets a concentrated three-level public building. This taller element places reception functions below educational assistance facilities and a top-floor library, giving the composition its most prominent upward expression.

Three mutually connected buildings create a tightly arranged triangular configuration. One combines communal activities at ground level with creative studios directly overhead, accommodating social events, presentations and practical artistic work. Another contains administrative and public functions beneath an uppermost library, while a straightforward classroom structure provides the third component. Direct internal links connect every pair of buildings.

The school is arranged as three consecutive structures along a single route. Classroom accommodation occupies one extremity and communal facilities the other. Between them, a central administrative and cultural building contains reception, offices, creative teaching rooms and the library. It provides the main entrance and principal circulation junction, requiring anyone moving between the two outer buildings to pass through this middle section.

Nearly all routine educational activities take place within one substantial teaching building, which accommodates the main entrance on its lowest level and the library at its highest. An adjacent single-level structure provides practical creative workspaces and operational facilities. Positioned between the teaching building and assembly hall, this smaller element establishes their connection while concentrating fabrication activities and building services at that intermediate point.

Three buildings of equal three-level height form a closely connected arrangement surrounding an outdoor court, with direct connections between all three. The assembly facilities occupy a building of the same vertical extent as its neighbors, incorporating upper-level creative studios over the utility area with views toward the performance platform. The remaining buildings accommodate classrooms and administration, with additional educational assistance rooms adjacent to the office and health facilities.

Communal activities occupy the principal connecting structure, containing spaces for recreation, meals and schoolwide events, with visual and performing arts studios situated overhead. A classroom building and a separate entrance-and-assistance building extend from this shared facility. Neither outer building connects directly to the other, making the communal structure the necessary route for movement between instructional accommodation and administrative or inclusive services.

An assembly and activity building occupies the middle of the composition, receiving two separate extensions from opposing directions. One contains a full range of classroom facilities together with dedicated creative teaching rooms. The smaller extension houses reception and administration on its lower level and the library upstairs. No direct connection exists between these extensions; circulation from one to the other must traverse the central gathering facility.

The school operates as three distinct buildings distributed across a common site, without enclosed corridors linking them. One independently functioning teaching building includes routine student welfare provision. A second accommodates sport and meals and can operate separately for neighborhood use. The third is a shorter administration-and-creative-education building located at the entrance, placing the library over the offices. All transfers between buildings take place outside.

Three directly interconnected structures surround a common open-air space. The tallest accommodates teaching rooms on floors above the administrative entrance facilities, with the library occupying its uppermost level. A neighboring building combines additional educational assistance, healthcare and creative instruction. The communal building provides the remaining side, completing a continuous enclosed circulation arrangement in which each structure connects independently with both others.

The principal school consists of two neighboring elongated teaching buildings running alongside one another and connected directly. The first accommodates general classrooms and places the library on its highest level. The second combines reception and administrative functions with additional inclusive educational provision. A separate assembly and community facility occupies the same grounds without a built connection to either teaching building.

A short administrative and cultural building occupies the space between a three-level classroom structure and a communal assembly facility. This intermediate section provides their sole internal connection and accommodates the school's principal entrance. Reception, practical creative activities and library provision are concentrated where visitors enter, with teaching accommodation extending in one direction and the shared gathering facility in the other.

Three buildings follow a straight progression from a relatively secluded classroom structure to a communal assembly facility. Between these endpoints stands a concentrated entrance building containing administration at its lowest level and creative instruction and library accommodation above. This middle section serves as the main public arrival point and obligatory internal route between teaching areas and the assembly facility.

A communal building occupies the midpoint of the school, connecting an entrance-and-administration section on one side with classroom accommodation on the other. The two outer sections have no direct link. Visitors first enter the common activity space before reaching the teaching section beyond, separating classrooms from immediate public access. Creative subjects are incorporated into the classroom section alongside regular instruction.

The complete daily instructional program occupies a single independently functioning elongated building. Administrative reception and additional educational services occupy its lowest portion, classrooms rise above them, and the library completes the uppermost level. Elsewhere on the same property stand two physically separate structures: one for communal assemblies and another for practical creative work and upkeep operations. Access between all three requires outdoor travel.

Three connected building sections surround an open-air quadrangle, with enclosed links at each junction providing an uninterrupted circulation circuit. The classroom section rises higher than the others, while a shorter entrance section accommodates administration and creative instruction. The third section contains communal gathering facilities, with an elevated library space above the assembly area oriented toward the interior outdoor space.
